notes:
I've written notes for most of the chapter, but there are real gaps. I couldn't open the Enduring Word page (Guzik's comments below are quoted by Precept Austin). The Jamieson, Fausset & Brown page loaded without any commentary text. I found nothing on these sites from Methodist/Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Lutheran, Catholic or Orthodox teachers, or from modern scholars (Bible Odyssey, NET Bible notes). So the "traditions differ" points rely on Reformed, Baptist, Presbyterian and Anglican writers, plus older commentators. Verses 2, 12–14 and 20 had almost nothing usable.

**v. 1**
- In this verse Paul doesn't call himself an apostle or the church's founder. He points to Christ and calls himself and Timothy "servants."  https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8
- **Overseers and deacons: one point where traditions differ.**
  - Gill (Baptist): the overseers were ordinary local pastors, all equal, not regional bishops. He says the only offices God set up are pastors and deacons, and calls anything added "without warrant."  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/1-1.html  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/1.htm
  - Barnes (Presbyterian): the word is plural, so it can't mean a bishop over a region. He cites Jerome that bishop and presbyter were once the same office, and concludes the apostles organised at least one church without a "prelate" (a senior bishop over other clergy).  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/1.htm  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/philippians/1-1.html
  - Anglican scholars: Lightfoot found it "incredible" that Paul would greet only bishops and deacons if presbyters were a separate order, so the two must be the same. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/philippians-1.html F. B. Meyer quotes Lightfoot, Ellicott and Moule saying the New Testament uses "bishop" and "elder" for the same officer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcp/philippians-1.html
  - Poole notes that the Church of England's ordination service still calls deacons "ministers." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/1.htm
  - Jamieson, Fausset & Brown suggest that once the apostles were gone, one presbyter came to preside and took the title "bishop" in the later, narrower sense. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Phl/Phl_001.cfm (from the search snippet)
  - GotQuestions (evangelical): elders and bishops were the same; churches were led by a group of elders plus deacons. https://www.gotquestions.org/church-government.html
  - Constable: the church had several elders and several deacons. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philippians/1-1.html
- Paul writes to the whole congregation rather than to its leaders. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Phl/Phl_001.cfm

**vv. 3–5**
- "Upon every remembrance" means the Philippians themselves are the reason for Paul's thanks, not just the moments he remembers them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_13-5
- Matt Chandler: this is Paul's only letter that doesn't correct bad teaching or behaviour. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_13-5
- Paul thanks God, not the church, because God is the source of joy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_13-5

**v. 6** (debated)
- Traditional reading: Paul was sure the work would last because God began it. He uses a Greek tense that shows a settled conviction. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8
- Hendriksen: Paul ties the church's faithfulness ("partnership… until now") closely to God keeping them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8
- Spurgeon said he believed in "the final perseverance of God." https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8
- Reformed view:
  - Ligonier: if you truly have saving faith you will never lose it, and if you lose it you never had it. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/tulip-and-reformed-theology-perseverance-saints
  - Monergism quotes the Westminster Confession: true believers cannot totally or finally fall away. https://www.monergism.com/topics/perseverance-saints/perseverance-saints
  - Boice counts this verse among the three greatest texts for the doctrine. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-3-confident-about-salvation-philippians-13-6
- Piper (Baptist, Reformed) adds a qualification: perseverance is a real condition, and those who don't persevere will be lost. Believers are secure because God makes sure they persevere, not because the condition is removed. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/perseverance-of-the-saints-session-8
- The Arminian view, which is the usual Methodist and Wesleyan position, appears here only as its Reformed critic A. A. Hodge describes it: keeping one's faith depends on the believer's free will, so a believer can fall away. Hodge also cites the Catholic Council of Trent condemning the Reformed position. These describe opponents, so they aren't those traditions speaking for themselves. https://www.monergism.com/perseverance-saints-1
- Augustine (on New Advent) asks whether this verse ever stopped Paul from urging people to keep going. He treats perseverance as God's gift. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/15122.htm
- Debated modern teaching: The Gospel Coalition criticises "free grace theology," in which perseverance affects only heavenly rewards, not final salvation. It calls this an unstable middle position. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/preservation-and-perseverance/

**vv. 7–8**
- "Have you in my heart" is in the present tense, so they are always on his heart. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8
- The church shared his work through repeated gifts despite its poverty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8
- Matthew Henry: Paul's longing copies the compassion of Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8

**vv. 9–11**
- Knowledge and discernment, not warm feelings, should be the ground of love. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61076/
- Beet: "more and more" politely admits their love is already rich in knowledge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61076/
- Constable: we can stand blameless only if the Spirit controls us. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61076/
- Eadie: the fruit is not self-produced but comes through Christ's work by the Spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61076/

**vv. 12–14**
- Paul talks about God's purposes rather than his own problems. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8

**vv. 15–17**
- These rivals preached the real gospel. Olford says they were not heretics or Judaizers (who required Gentile converts to keep the Jewish law), just jealous. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61066/
- Their message was right but their motive was wrong, which is a warning for the Philippians. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_115-17
- The application drawn is to check your own motives in ministry. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61066/

**vv. 18–19**
- "Deliverance" can mean rescue from danger or salvation. Either way, Paul knew his trouble was temporary. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8
- Paul relies on prayer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8

**v. 21**
- One sermon's summary of "to die is gain": at death we lose sin and sorrow, keep our identity, and gain heaven and Christ's presence. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_17-8

**vv. 22–24** (debated: what happens at death)
- Barnes: the Christian's soul goes straight to Christ at death, and the soul does not sleep. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/1-23.htm
- Gill makes the same point. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/philippians/1-23.html
- Ellicott: the dead are usually described as at "rest," but this verse shows a rest with conscious fellowship with Christ. The Greek means "far, far better." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/philippians/1-23.htm
- Another older note: compared with the final resurrection, the rest of the righteous dead is like sleep. https://biblehub.com/philippians/1-23.htm
- Desiring God: believers stay conscious between death and resurrection. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-do-you-believe-about-the-intermediate-state
- Berkhof (Reformed): some Reformed theologians held that believers wait in an in-between place until the resurrection, but he says Scripture puts the soul with Christ. https://www.monergism.com/intermediate-state
- Precept Austin reads the verse as ruling out both soul sleep and purgatory. That is a Protestant argument; I found no Catholic source on this verse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_121-24

**vv. 25–26**
- Wuest: Paul became convinced they needed him more than he needed heaven, so he expected to be released. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_125-30
- Steven Cole: they will boast in Christ, not in Paul. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_125-30

**vv. 27–28**
- "Conduct" (KJV "conversation") means how you live, not what you say. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_127-28
- "The faith" here means what is believed: the gospel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_127-28
- Their fearlessness is a sign to their persecutors, not to themselves. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_127-28

**vv. 29–30**
- Brian Bill: this verse corrects the American Christian habit of talking mainly about blessing, prosperity and God's favour. This is the closest I found to a response to prosperity teaching. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_129-30
- Guzik: their trials were a tool in God's hand, not a punishment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_129-30
- Suffering doesn't save, but it is a clear sign of salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_129-30
- Spurgeon calls suffering for Christ a gift to rejoice in. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_129-30

The next sources to check, if you can open them directly, are enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philippians-1/, the Bible Hub commentary pages for each verse, and New Advent or Catholic.com for verses 1 and 23.
